blocks.text: **The problem.** You are given an m × n matrix in which every row is sorted in ascending order, and the first value of each row is greater than the last value of the row before it. Given a `target`, return `true` if it is in the matrix and `false` otherwise — in **O(log(m × n))** time.

blocks.alt: A 3 by 4 matrix whose rows, read one after another, form one sorted list: 1, 3, 5, 7, 10, 11, 16, 20, 23, 30, 34, 60. Each row is a different colour.

blocks.text: The two sorting rules together say something strong: if you read the matrix **row by row**, left to right, you get **one long sorted list**. That's the whole problem — once you see it, you can use ordinary binary search.

items: **Check every cell** — O(m × n). Ignores the sorting entirely.
**Binary search each row** — O(m log n). Better, but still visits every row.
**Binary search for the row, then within the row** — O(log m + log n). Fast, but two searches to get right.
**Binary search the whole matrix as one list** — O(log(m × n)), and only one search to write.

blocks.text: The key insight: a position is a (row, column) pair in disguise

Number the cells `0` to `m × n − 1` in reading order. Position `i` lives at row `i / n` (integer division) and column `i % n`. So binary-search the positions, and convert the middle position to a cell only when you need its value.

blocks.alt: Position 5 in reading order, with 4 columns per row, is row 5 ÷ 4 = 1 and column 5 % 4 = 1: the value 11.

blocks.text: The faded cells have been ruled out. Try a target that's in the matrix and one that isn't — you'll need at most about log₂(m × n) steps either way.

blocks.alt: Scanning every cell: O(m × n). Binary search over all positions: O(log(m × n)) time and O(1) space.

blocks.text: Each step halves the remaining positions: **O(log(m × n)) time, O(1) space**. For a 1000 × 1000 matrix that's about 20 steps instead of a million.

items: **Target smaller than everything** or **larger than everything** — returns false quickly.
**One row** or **one column** — the same code works.
**Target equal to the first or last value** — check the loop uses `low <= high`.

blocks.text: A cousin you'll meet: Search a 2D Matrix II

If the rows are sorted and the **columns** are sorted, but rows don't continue each other, the "one long list" trick breaks. Instead, start at the **top-right corner**: if the value is too big, move left; if it's too small, move down. Each step rules out a whole row or column, giving **O(m + n)** time.
